title: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in all cells whatsoever, the process of division must somehow be explained as the result of a conflict between surface-tension and its opposing forces.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Cell division and surface tension”. Scope: all dividing cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specific mechanical models are testable in selected animal and plant systems. Existing data cannot establish the claim for all cells, and its broad wording weakens discrimination.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across representative cell types, quantify cortical or interfacial tension and opposing spindle, ring, adhesion, and pressure forces during division, then test whether force-balance models predict furrow position and equatorial division. A division mode not involving a relevant surface-tension balance would refute the universal claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Surface tension is not directly measured in most imaging datasets.

The universal scope includes highly divergent cell walls and division mechanisms.

A broad force-balance description can be hard to falsify.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Furrow position relative to the spindle is widely imaged and can be scored now. The force claim, a conflict with surface tension in every cell, depends on mechanical measurements that are scattered and taxonomically narrow. Active ring contractility is a rival that those limited experiments can sometimes separate from passive surface tension, so the test is informative only inside that subset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: During cytokinesis, decompose the force across the furrow into cortical surface tension and other contributions such as an actomyosin ring, and check that the division plane is the equator of the spindle. Division that proceeds when surface tension is held constant, driven by active contractility, would refute a necessary conflict with surface tension; a furrow that appears only when surface tension yields at that equator would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim says all cells, while force data exist for a handful of model types.

Cortical tension and active contractility are easily conflated.

Image repositories record shape much more often than tension.
